title: The Confluence
subtitle: Hierarchical Clustering · hclust + cutree + summarise
story: You came down into the red canyon to map its springs, and the flood season came early. Sheltering, you find a stair into a drowned hall the old makers left behind — their floodworks, a single sealed tunnel that climbs to safety, an engraved panel no living hand has set, and a map of the whole canyon with every height left blank. A ladder climbs from the hall to the high springs. The makers built this place to be run by someone who could read the canyon as they did — its waters sorted into families, its channels into one branching tree. Climb, and roam the whole canyon: read the springs at each junction to learn which waters are kin, and mark each junction's height on your map as you pass it. Then come back down to the hall and read the shape of the land itself — before the water climbs to meet you.

done.title: The map lied
done.body: The carved map grouped the springs by the fork they rise in — but two springs' water swore a different kin, and you saw it. The storm breaks; the canyon fills. Kinship hides beneath the surface, and only the reading finds it. Back down to the hall — the panel is waiting, and your map of heights is full.

escapeDone.title: Free of the canyon
escapeDone.body: You draw the waterline across your map and count the canyon's severed limbs — and the panel takes it. You throw the great wheel; a sluice grinds, the flood turns aside, and the sealed tunnel opens. You climb as the hall drowns behind you, into rain and open sky. The canyon kept its one promise: read me truly, and go free.

coverPrompt: Minimalist stylised thumbnail poster of a lone red slot-canyon: a single narrow cleft in dark sandstone opening downward into a branching gorge, one warm amber light glowing deep in the rock below, a cool teal storm-sky above. One bold high-contrast silhouette, iconic and uncluttered, minimal detail. Flat limited palette: deep teal, icy blue, one warm amber glow. Soft film grain, painterly but clean, strong negative space, single centred focal subject. No people, no text, no lettering, no logos. Square composition.

debrief.title: How this world worked
debrief.intro: The whole canyon was one skill in disguise: sorting many things into a nested tree of families by how alike they are. Each junction taught one move of hierarchical clustering, and the escape was the move made physical — reading the true branching structure of the land and cutting it into groups.

rooms.title: The drowned hall

Directly behind the viewer, split across the extreme left and extreme right edges, is a plain unbroken stretch of wet red-sandstone wall in deep shadow, near-black and featureless, uniform and unlit: the far-left edge and the far-right edge are the two halves of this one surface and must match exactly in colour, texture, and lighting, joining into a single continuous, unbroken whole when the image wraps left to right. entry.title: The drowned hall
entry.body: A stair takes you down out of the rising wind into a hall no living hand tends. An engraved panel you cannot read. A blank map you roll and pocket. A sealed tunnel that will not open. And a ladder, climbing up into the canyon. Start by climbing — and mark every junction's height as you go.

rooms.designNote: FRAME ROOM (no graded puzzle). Cold open: seed the mystery — the PANEL (clue, unreadable now; pays off at 'works') and the blank MAP (clue, pickup; the escape's reading surface). Passages: a LADDER up to j_c1 (the high springs) and a TRUNK arch to j_c7. Both UNGATED. NEW ART; the escape room 'works' REUSES this scene (water higher, panel lit). MAZE MODEL (engine work Lucas will build): every passage is OPEN from the start (roam freely, backtrack anytime); a puzzle at a junction is served next-in-queue via availableWhen (a diegetic 'not yet' if out of order); the survey is DRY so nothing seals off; the escape panel refuses an INCOMPLETE map, so the player goes back for any junction whose height is still blank. Scene shows OPEN fork-passages (no closed-door art needed on maze passages) — only the escape tunnel is a gated closed->open door.

rooms.designNote: ESCAPE (data-free meta-echo; the cut). MECHANIC (current engine): a LOCK whose code is the panel's missing row, read off the wall MAP (a clue showing the confluence tree + the heights the player gathered: c1 1400, c2 1380, c4 1420, c5 1390, LEFT-mid c3 1050, RIGHT-mid c6 1200, trunk c7 850). The panel gives three flood-heights x cluster sizes; two rows lit, one dark: HIGH 1300 -> 2,2,2,2 (lit); LOW 950 -> 4,4 (lit); MIDDLE 1125 -> ? (dark). Player draws the 1125 waterline: above c3(1050), below c6(1200) -> the RIGHT half stays whole (4) while the LEFT splits (2,2) => 2,2,4. LOCK ANSWER = '224' (left-to-right across the canyon). Verified: _scratch/verify_escape_topology.py. NO data/CSV — heights are world props. EXIT tunnel requires the lock; ALSO gate on MAP-COMPLETENESS (all 7 junction heights read) — engine. REUSES 'undercroft' scene (water higher, panel lit). MAZE MODEL (engine work Lucas will build): every passage is OPEN from the start (roam freely, backtrack anytime); a puzzle at a junction is served next-in-queue via availableWhen (a diegetic 'not yet' if out of order); the survey is DRY so nothing seals off; the escape panel refuses an INCOMPLETE map, so the player goes back for any junction whose height is still blank. Scene shows OPEN fork-passages (no closed-door art needed on maze passages) — only the escape tunnel is a gated closed->open door. FUTURE UPGRADE: replace the lock with the draggable-node map + live matrix-grid panel (puzzle_inventory #19).
